title: Information-Theoretic Watermark Channels: Bounding What a Model Can Covertly Signal

original_idea.body:
# Information-Theoretic Watermark Channels: Bounding What a Model Can Covertly Signal

**Problem:** A theoretical open problem is proving limits on what AI systems can hide or covertly reveal; in particular, how much information one model instance can smuggle to another through ostensibly-benign outputs.

**Direction:** Import covert-channel capacity analysis from information theory / security. Set up two open-model instances where one must encode a secret bitstring into a constrained, monitored text channel and the other decodes it, with a simple monitor trying to detect anomalies. Empirically estimate the covert channel capacity (bits per message at a fixed detection rate) and how it shrinks as the monitor tightens.

**Why it matters:** Directly operationalizes the AISI open problem of proving limits on what AI can hide, yielding measured covert-channel capacities under realistic monitoring. Pure inference + simple stats; no lab infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** Covert-channel capacity is a classic information-theory/security notion. UK AISI open problem: prove theoretical limits on what AI systems can hide, reveal, or prove about their behavior. Connects to steganographic collusion concerns.
